Tracking Spending

TipHow these exercises work

Each topic starts with a real scenario and a bar model, then three levels of exercises. Level 1 (Guided) fills in the blanks of a finished function. Level 2 (Practice) applies it to new numbers. Level 3 (Challenge) asks a new question with little scaffolding. The R and Python exercises run in your browser: click Run Code to try, Submit Answer to check, and use the hint or solution if you get stuck. Excel exercises have a solution you can reveal.

Book Topics

  • Tracking vs. budgeting: tracking records where money actually went; budgeting allocates where it should go; comparing the two creates a feedback loop
  • Capture methods: spending journal, checkbook register, cash envelopes, bank statements; pick one and run it for a full month
  • Categorizing: start with about 10 stable buckets (housing, transportation, groceries, dining out, subscriptions, personal, health, gifts, fun money, other); when in doubt use “Other”, and only promote a new category after seeing it three months in a row
  • Using spreadsheets: bank exports have Date, Description, and Amount columns; a keyword lookup adds the Category column in one pass
  • Monthly review: pull, categorize, compare to budget, and pick one change for next month
  • Online subscriptions: Americans spend about $219/month on subscriptions and underestimate it by $133; audit every quarter and cancel anything unused in 30 days
  • Math: the subscription audit, the opportunity cost of a $20/month subscription invested at 7% for 30 years (about $22,700)

Bank Statement Data

A minimal bank export has three columns: Date, Description, and Amount. The code blocks below show how to create an example bank statement file in R, Python, and Excel.

  • Excel
  • Python
  • R

We can simply copy and paste the data into Excel; Date in A, Description in B, Amount in C.

In Python, we’ll use polars to create a DataFrame and display the bank statement. This is similar to the tibble we created above.

Categorizing Transactions

A bank export only says where the money went (Description). Adding a Category column turns a list of merchants into budget buckets. In R, dplyr::case_when() checks each rule in order and the first match wins; in Python, numpy.select() does the same with a list of conditions and a list of labels; in Excel, IFS() does it one cell at a time. Anything that matches no rule falls into “Other”.

Level 1: Guided

Fill in the blanks so grocery stores (Trader Joe’s, Whole Foods, Costco) become “Groceries” and everything without a rule becomes “Other”. How many transactions are groceries?

  • Excel
  • Python
  • R

With Description in column B, write an IFS() formula in D2 that labels subscriptions, groceries, and “Other”, then fill it down and count the groceries.

NoteSolution

SEARCH() finds a keyword in a cell, ISNUMBER() turns that into true/false, and OR() joins several keywords. The final TRUE, "Other" catches everything else.

=IFS(
  OR(ISNUMBER(SEARCH("Netflix",B2)),ISNUMBER(SEARCH("Spotify",B2)),ISNUMBER(SEARCH("NYTimes",B2)),ISNUMBER(SEARCH("24 Hour Fitness",B2))), "Subscriptions",
  OR(ISNUMBER(SEARCH("Trader Joe",B2)),ISNUMBER(SEARCH("Whole Foods",B2)),ISNUMBER(SEARCH("Costco",B2))), "Groceries",
  TRUE, "Other"
)

Then count them with =COUNTIF(D:D, "Groceries"). The answer is 3.

#| exercise: cat_1_py
#| setup: true
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
statement = pd.DataFrame({
    "Description": [
        "Employer Payroll", "Rent", "Comcast Internet", "Trader Joe's",
        "Shell Gas", "Netflix", "Starbucks", "PG&E Electric",
        "AT&T Wireless", "Spotify", "Whole Foods", "Chipotle",
        "Geico Auto Insurance", "NYTimes Digital", "Shell Gas", "Costco",
        "24 Hour Fitness"],
    "Amount": [
         2400.00, -1500.00, -75.00, -82.45, -45.20, -15.99, -6.75,
        -142.30, -85.00, -10.99, -64.12, -14.50, -125.00, -17.00,
         -42.80, -156.78, -39.99]
})
#| exercise: cat_1_py
desc = statement["Description"]
statement["Category"] = np.select(
    [desc.str.contains("Netflix|Spotify|NYTimes|24 Hour Fitness"),
     desc.str.contains(______)],
    ["Subscriptions", "Groceries"],
    default=______
)
(statement["Category"] == "Groceries").sum()

Separate the store names with | (it means “or”): "Trader Joe|Whole Foods|Costco". The default label is "Other".

Solution. 

desc = statement["Description"]
statement["Category"] = np.select(
    [desc.str.contains("Netflix|Spotify|NYTimes|24 Hour Fitness"),
     desc.str.contains("Trader Joe|Whole Foods|Costco")],
    ["Subscriptions", "Groceries"],
    default="Other"
)
(statement["Category"] == "Groceries").sum()
#| exercise: cat_1_py
#| check: true
if result == 3:
    feedback = {"correct": True, "message": "Right: Trader Joe's, Whole Foods, and Costco."}
else:
    feedback = {"correct": False, "message": "Not quite. List all three stores, separated by |."}
feedback
#| exercise: cat_1_r
#| setup: true
library(dplyr)
statement <- data.frame(
  Description = c(
    "Employer Payroll", "Rent", "Comcast Internet", "Trader Joe's",
    "Shell Gas", "Netflix", "Starbucks", "PG&E Electric",
    "AT&T Wireless", "Spotify", "Whole Foods", "Chipotle",
    "Geico Auto Insurance", "NYTimes Digital", "Shell Gas", "Costco",
    "24 Hour Fitness"),
  Amount = c(
     2400.00, -1500.00, -75.00, -82.45, -45.20, -15.99, -6.75,
    -142.30, -85.00, -10.99, -64.12, -14.50, -125.00, -17.00,
     -42.80, -156.78, -39.99)
)
#| exercise: cat_1_r
statement |>
  mutate(Category = case_when(
    grepl("Netflix|Spotify|NYTimes|24 Hour Fitness", Description) ~ "Subscriptions",
    grepl(______, Description) ~ "Groceries",
    TRUE ~ ______
  )) |>
  filter(Category == "Groceries") |>
  nrow()

Separate the store names with | (it means “or”): "Trader Joe|Whole Foods|Costco". The last rule’s label is "Other".

Solution. 

statement |>
  mutate(Category = case_when(
    grepl("Netflix|Spotify|NYTimes|24 Hour Fitness", Description) ~ "Subscriptions",
    grepl("Trader Joe|Whole Foods|Costco", Description) ~ "Groceries",
    TRUE ~ "Other"
  )) |>
  filter(Category == "Groceries") |>
  nrow()
#| exercise: cat_1_r
#| check: true
if (isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(.result), 3))) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Right: Trader Joe's, Whole Foods, and Costco.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Not quite. List all three stores, separated by |.")
}

Level 2: Practice

Next month’s export has three new merchants: Safeway (groceries), Hulu (a subscription), and Uber (transportation). The rules below don’t know them yet, so they land in “Other”. Update the rules so no transaction is left in “Other”.

  • Excel
  • Python
  • R

Your IFS() formula labels the new month’s Safeway, Hulu, and Uber rows as “Other”. Edit it so =COUNTIF(D:D, "Other") returns 0.

NoteSolution

Add each new merchant to its group with another ISNUMBER(SEARCH(...)) inside the OR(), and add a Transportation rule:

OR(..., ISNUMBER(SEARCH("Safeway",B2))), "Groceries",
OR(..., ISNUMBER(SEARCH("Hulu",B2))), "Subscriptions",
OR(ISNUMBER(SEARCH("Shell",B2)),ISNUMBER(SEARCH("Uber",B2))), "Transportation",

Re-fill the formula down after editing it.

#| exercise: cat_2_py
#| setup: true
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
statement = pd.DataFrame({
    "Description": ["Employer Payroll", "Rent", "Safeway", "Hulu",
                    "Netflix", "Uber Trip", "Shell Gas", "Chipotle"],
    "Amount": [2400.00, -1500.00, -71.20, -17.99, -15.99, -23.40, -44.10, -13.25]
})
#| exercise: cat_2_py
desc = statement["Description"]
statement["Category"] = np.select(
    [desc.str.contains("Payroll"),
     desc.str.contains("Rent"),
     desc.str.contains("Trader Joe|Whole Foods|Costco"),
     desc.str.contains("Netflix|Spotify|NYTimes|24 Hour Fitness"),
     desc.str.contains("Shell"),
     desc.str.contains("Starbucks|Chipotle")],
    ["Income", "Housing", "Groceries", "Subscriptions", "Transportation", "Dining"],
    default="Other"
)
(statement["Category"] == "Other").sum()

Add each new merchant to the pattern for its group, separated by |. For example, "Shell|Uber".

Solution. 

desc = statement["Description"]
statement["Category"] = np.select(
    [desc.str.contains("Payroll"),
     desc.str.contains("Rent"),
     desc.str.contains("Trader Joe|Whole Foods|Costco|Safeway"),
     desc.str.contains("Netflix|Spotify|NYTimes|24 Hour Fitness|Hulu"),
     desc.str.contains("Shell|Uber"),
     desc.str.contains("Starbucks|Chipotle")],
    ["Income", "Housing", "Groceries", "Subscriptions", "Transportation", "Dining"],
    default="Other"
)
(statement["Category"] == "Other").sum()
#| exercise: cat_2_py
#| check: true
if result == 0:
    feedback = {"correct": True, "message": "Right: every transaction has a home."}
else:
    feedback = {"correct": False, "message": f"{result} transaction(s) are still 'Other'. Check Safeway, Hulu, and Uber."}
feedback
#| exercise: cat_2_r
#| setup: true
library(dplyr)
statement <- data.frame(
  Description = c("Employer Payroll", "Rent", "Safeway", "Hulu",
                  "Netflix", "Uber Trip", "Shell Gas", "Chipotle"),
  Amount = c(2400.00, -1500.00, -71.20, -17.99, -15.99, -23.40, -44.10, -13.25)
)
#| exercise: cat_2_r
statement |>
  mutate(Category = case_when(
    grepl("Payroll", Description) ~ "Income",
    grepl("Rent", Description) ~ "Housing",
    grepl("Trader Joe|Whole Foods|Costco", Description) ~ "Groceries",
    grepl("Netflix|Spotify|NYTimes|24 Hour Fitness", Description) ~ "Subscriptions",
    grepl("Shell", Description) ~ "Transportation",
    grepl("Starbucks|Chipotle", Description) ~ "Dining",
    TRUE ~ "Other"
  )) |>
  filter(Category == "Other") |>
  nrow()

Add each new merchant to the pattern for its group, separated by |. For example, "Shell|Uber".

Solution. 

statement |>
  mutate(Category = case_when(
    grepl("Payroll", Description) ~ "Income",
    grepl("Rent", Description) ~ "Housing",
    grepl("Trader Joe|Whole Foods|Costco|Safeway", Description) ~ "Groceries",
    grepl("Netflix|Spotify|NYTimes|24 Hour Fitness|Hulu", Description) ~ "Subscriptions",
    grepl("Shell|Uber", Description) ~ "Transportation",
    grepl("Starbucks|Chipotle", Description) ~ "Dining",
    TRUE ~ "Other"
  )) |>
  filter(Category == "Other") |>
  nrow()
#| exercise: cat_2_r
#| check: true
if (isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(.result), 0))) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Right: every transaction has a home.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = paste(.result, "transaction(s) are still 'Other'. Check Safeway, Hulu, and Uber."))
}

Level 3: Challenge

Real bank exports are messy: the same merchant can show up as NETFLIX.COM, Netflix, or netflix. The rule below only matches the exact capitalization, so it finds just 1 of the 3 subscriptions. Change the code so capitalization doesn’t matter, and count the subscriptions again.

  • Excel
  • Python
  • R

Does the IFS() and SEARCH() formula need any change for NETFLIX.COM?

NoteSolution

No. SEARCH() ignores capitalization, so SEARCH("Netflix", "NETFLIX.COM") already finds a match. (Its case-sensitive cousin is FIND().)

#| exercise: cat_3_py
#| setup: true
import pandas as pd
messy = pd.DataFrame({
    "Description": ["NETFLIX.COM", "Spotify USA", "nytimes digital",
                    "SHELL OIL 1234", "Whole Foods #102"],
    "Amount": [-15.99, -10.99, -17.00, -45.20, -64.12]
})
#| exercise: cat_3_py
is_sub = messy["Description"].str.contains("Netflix|Spotify|NYTimes|24 Hour Fitness")
is_sub.sum()

str.contains() has a case argument. Look at what case=False does.

Solution. 

is_sub = messy["Description"].str.contains("Netflix|Spotify|NYTimes|24 Hour Fitness", case=False)
is_sub.sum()
#| exercise: cat_3_py
#| check: true
if result == 3:
    feedback = {"correct": True, "message": "Right: all three subscriptions, whatever the capitalization."}
else:
    feedback = {"correct": False, "message": "Not quite. Make the match ignore capitalization."}
feedback
#| exercise: cat_3_r
#| setup: true
library(dplyr)
messy <- data.frame(
  Description = c("NETFLIX.COM", "Spotify USA", "nytimes digital",
                  "SHELL OIL 1234", "Whole Foods #102"),
  Amount = c(-15.99, -10.99, -17.00, -45.20, -64.12)
)
#| exercise: cat_3_r
messy |>
  filter(grepl("Netflix|Spotify|NYTimes|24 Hour Fitness", Description)) |>
  nrow()

grepl() has an ignore.case argument.

Solution. 

messy |>
  filter(grepl("Netflix|Spotify|NYTimes|24 Hour Fitness", Description, ignore.case = TRUE)) |>
  nrow()
#| exercise: cat_3_r
#| check: true
if (isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(.result), 3))) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Right: all three subscriptions, whatever the capitalization.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Not quite. Make the match ignore capitalization.")
}

Answering Tracking Questions

Once every row has a category, the book’s three tracking questions take one short pipeline each: what did subscriptions cost, what share of income went to fixed costs, and which variable category was biggest? Spending is stored as negative numbers, so a minus sign turns a spending total positive.

Level 1: Guided

What did the four subscriptions cost this month?

  • Excel
  • Python
  • R

With Amount in C and Category in D, total the subscriptions as a positive number.

NoteSolution 
=-SUMIF(D:D, "Subscriptions", C:C)

This returns $83.97.

#| exercise: q_1_py
#| setup: true
import pandas as pd
statement = pd.DataFrame({
    "Description": [
        "Employer Payroll", "Rent", "Comcast Internet", "Trader Joe's",
        "Shell Gas", "Netflix", "Starbucks", "PG&E Electric",
        "AT&T Wireless", "Spotify", "Whole Foods", "Chipotle",
        "Geico Auto Insurance", "NYTimes Digital", "Shell Gas", "Costco",
        "24 Hour Fitness"],
    "Amount": [
         2400.00, -1500.00, -75.00, -82.45, -45.20, -15.99, -6.75,
        -142.30, -85.00, -10.99, -64.12, -14.50, -125.00, -17.00,
         -42.80, -156.78, -39.99],
    "Category": [
        "Income", "Housing", "Utilities", "Groceries", "Transportation",
        "Subscriptions", "Dining", "Utilities", "Utilities", "Subscriptions",
        "Groceries", "Dining", "Insurance", "Subscriptions", "Transportation",
        "Groceries", "Subscriptions"]
})
#| exercise: q_1_py
-statement.loc[statement["Category"] == ______, "Amount"].sum()

Pick the rows whose Category is "Subscriptions".

Solution. 

-statement.loc[statement["Category"] == "Subscriptions", "Amount"].sum()
#| exercise: q_1_py
#| check: true
if result is not None and abs(result - 83.97) < 0.01:
    feedback = {"correct": True, "message": "Right: $83.97 a month."}
else:
    feedback = {"correct": False, "message": "Not quite. Filter to Subscriptions and keep the minus sign."}
feedback

#| setup: true
library(dplyr)
statement <- data.frame(
  Description = c(
    "Employer Payroll", "Rent", "Comcast Internet", "Trader Joe's",
    "Shell Gas", "Netflix", "Starbucks", "PG&E Electric",
    "AT&T Wireless", "Spotify", "Whole Foods", "Chipotle",
    "Geico Auto Insurance", "NYTimes Digital", "Shell Gas", "Costco",
    "24 Hour Fitness"),
  Amount = c(
     2400.00, -1500.00, -75.00, -82.45, -45.20, -15.99, -6.75,
    -142.30, -85.00, -10.99, -64.12, -14.50, -125.00, -17.00,
     -42.80, -156.78, -39.99),
  Category = c(
    "Income", "Housing", "Utilities", "Groceries", "Transportation",
    "Subscriptions", "Dining", "Utilities", "Utilities", "Subscriptions",
    "Groceries", "Dining", "Insurance", "Subscriptions", "Transportation",

statement |>
  filter(Category == ______) |>
  summarise(total = -sum(Amount)) |>

Keep the rows whose Category is "Subscriptions".

Solution. 

statement |>
  filter(Category == "Subscriptions") |>
  summarise(total = -sum(Amount)) |>
  pull(total)
#| exercise: q_1_r
#| check: true
if (isTRUE(all.equal(.result, 83.97))) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Right: $83.97 a month.")

Level 2: Practice

Fixed costs are housing, utilities, and insurance. What share of income went to fixed costs? Give the answer as a decimal (for example, 0.25 for 25%).

  • Excel
  • Python
  • R

Total the three fixed categories and divide by income (the positive amounts).

NoteSolution 
=-(SUMIF(D:D,"Housing",C:C)+SUMIF(D:D,"Utilities",C:C)+SUMIF(D:D,"Insurance",C:C))/SUMIF(C:C,">0")

This returns 0.803, or about 80%.

#| exercise: q_2_py
#| setup: true
import pandas as pd
statement = pd.DataFrame({
    "Amount": [
         2400.00, -1500.00, -75.00, -82.45, -45.20, -15.99, -6.75,
        -142.30, -85.00, -10.99, -64.12, -14.50, -125.00, -17.00,
         -42.80, -156.78, -39.99],
    "Category": [
        "Income", "Housing", "Utilities", "Groceries", "Transportation",
        "Subscriptions", "Dining", "Utilities", "Utilities", "Subscriptions",
        "Groceries", "Dining", "Insurance", "Subscriptions", "Transportation",
        "Groceries", "Subscriptions"]
})
#| exercise: q_2_py
fixed = ["Housing", "Utilities", "Insurance"]
income = statement.loc[statement["Amount"] > 0, "Amount"].sum()
fixed_total = ______
fixed_total / income

statement["Category"].isin(fixed) picks the fixed-cost rows. Sum their Amount and flip the sign.

Solution. 

fixed = ["Housing", "Utilities", "Insurance"]
income = statement.loc[statement["Amount"] > 0, "Amount"].sum()
fixed_total = -statement.loc[statement["Category"].isin(fixed), "Amount"].sum()
fixed_total / income
#| exercise: q_2_py
#| check: true
if result is not None and abs(result - 0.8030) < 0.001:
    feedback = {"correct": True, "message": "Right: about 80%. This statement has the full month's rent but only one paycheck."}
else:
    feedback = {"correct": False, "message": "Not quite. Total housing, utilities, and insurance as a positive number."}
feedback
#| exercise: q_2_r
#| setup: true
library(dplyr)
statement <- data.frame(
  Amount = c(
     2400.00, -1500.00, -75.00, -82.45, -45.20, -15.99, -6.75,
    -142.30, -85.00, -10.99, -64.12, -14.50, -125.00, -17.00,
     -42.80, -156.78, -39.99),
  Category = c(
    "Income", "Housing", "Utilities", "Groceries", "Transportation",
    "Subscriptions", "Dining", "Utilities", "Utilities", "Subscriptions",
    "Groceries", "Dining", "Insurance", "Subscriptions", "Transportation",
    "Groceries", "Subscriptions")
)
#| exercise: q_2_r
fixed <- c("Housing", "Utilities", "Insurance")
income <- statement |> filter(Amount > 0) |> pull(Amount) |> sum()
fixed_total <- ______
fixed_total / income

filter(Category %in% fixed) keeps the fixed-cost rows; then summarise(total = -sum(Amount)) and pull(total).

Solution. 

fixed <- c("Housing", "Utilities", "Insurance")
income <- statement |> filter(Amount > 0) |> pull(Amount) |> sum()
fixed_total <- statement |> filter(Category %in% fixed) |> summarise(total = -sum(Amount)) |> pull(total)
fixed_total / income
#| exercise: q_2_r
#| check: true

Level 3: Challenge

Leaving out income, fixed costs, and subscriptions, which category had the most spending? Return its name.

Find the biggest variable category without scrolling through the rows.

NoteSolution

Select the data and use Insert → PivotTable with Category in Rows and Amount in Values, then sort smallest to largest (spending is negative). Or list the variable categories in F2:F4 (Groceries, Transportation, Dining), total each in G2 with =-SUMIF(D:D, F2, C:C), fill down, and use:

=INDEX(F2:F4, MATCH(MAX(G2:G4), G2:G4, 0))

The answer is Groceries ($303.35).

Filter out the skip categories with ~statement["Category"].isin(skip), then groupby("Category")["Amount"].sum(). Spending is negative, so the biggest is .idxmin().

variable.groupby("Category")["Amount"].sum().idxmin()

library(dplyr)

  Amount = c(
     2400.00, -1500.00, -75.00, -82.45, -45.20, -15.99, -6.75,
    -142.30, -85.00, -10.99, -64.12, -14.50, -125.00, -17.00,
     -42.80, -156.78, -39.99),
  Category = c(
    "Income", "Housing", "Utilities", "Groceries", "Transportation",
    "Subscriptions", "Dining", "Utilities", "Utilities", "Subscriptions",
    "Groceries", "Dining", "Insurance", "Subscriptions", "Transportation",
    "Groceries", "Subscriptions")
)
#| exercise: q_3_r
skip <- c("Income", "Housing", "Utilities", "Insurance", "Subscriptions")
# total spending by category, then return the name of the biggest

filter(!Category %in% skip), then group_by(Category) and summarise(Total = -sum(Amount)). Finish with slice_max(Total, n = 1) and pull(Category).

Solution. 

skip <- c("Income", "Housing", "Utilities", "Insurance", "Subscriptions")
statement |>
  filter(!Category %in% skip) |>
  group_by(Category) |>
  summarise(Total = -sum(Amount)) |>
  slice_max(Total, n = 1) |>
  pull(Category)
#| exercise: q_3_r
#| check: true
if (identical(as.character(.result), "Groceries")) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Right: Groceries, at $303.35.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Not quite. Return the category name with the largest spending total.")
}

The Subscription Audit Math

A $20/month subscription feels trivial. Cancel it and invest the $240 a year instead, and the chart below shows what that money grows into at each checkpoint, split into the money you put in and the growth it earned.

Formula: Annual cost × ((1 + r)^n − 1) ÷ r = Opportunity cost in n years

With the book’s 7% real return (the return after inflation), r = 0.07.

Each bar adds another year’s $240 to everything saved so far, and the whole pile grows by 7%. After 30 years you put in $7,200, and growth added about $15,500.

Level 1: Guided

Fill in the blanks to finish subscription_opportunity_cost(), then find what a $20/month subscription costs over 30 years at 7%.

  • Excel
  • Python
  • R

Put the monthly cost in A2 (20), the years in B2 (30), and the return in C2 (0.07). In D2, write the opportunity cost.

NoteSolution 
=(A2*12)*((1+C2)^B2-1)/C2

A2*12 turns the monthly cost into a yearly one. =FV(C2, B2, -A2*12) gives the same $22,670.59.

    annual_cost = monthly_cost * 12
    return annual_cost * ((1 + rate) ** years - 1) / rate

Find the 30-year value of $219 invested every month at 7%.

Use monthly_rate = rate / 12 and periods = years * 12, then the same formula with monthly_cost in place of the yearly amount.

Solution. 

def monthly_opportunity_cost(monthly_cost, years, rate=0.07):
    monthly_rate = rate / 12
    periods = years * 12
    return monthly_cost * ((1 + monthly_rate) ** periods - 1) / monthly_rate

monthly_opportunity_cost(219, 30)

monthly_opportunity_cost <- function(monthly_cost, years, rate = 0.07) {
  monthly_rate <- rate / 12
  periods      <- years * 12
  monthly_cost * ((1 + monthly_rate)^periods - 1) / monthly_rate
}
monthly_opportunity_cost(219, 30)
